articles.title: npm install prerender fails with "Failed to locate: CL.exe" on Windows: what it means and the fix
articles.author: Markus Delos Santos
articles.description:
You ran npm install for prerender on Windows, and the build stopped at "Failed to locate: CL.exe". CL.exe is Microsoft's C++ compiler, and the install couldn't find it. The fix is to install the Visual C++ build tools, then run npm install again from a Developer Command Prompt. And if all you wanted was the middleware for your app, check first whether you need this build at all.

Microsoft's docs describe cl.exe plainly: "Use the compiler (cl.exe) to compile and link source code files into apps, libraries, and DLLs." node-gyp, per its README, is "a cross-platform command-line tool written in Node.js for compiling native addon modules for Node.js." No compiler on the machine, no build.

Check which prerender package you actually need

This one is easy to miss. prerender-node describes itself as "Express middleware for prerendering javascript-rendered pages on the fly for SEO". That's the piece that goes in your app.

The prerender-node README says: "We host a Prerender server at prerender.io so that you can work on more important things." It also says the middleware "will default to the service already deployed by prerender.io". You can point it at a different service with the PRERENDER_SERVICE_URL environment variable or the prerenderServiceUrl option.

So if your goal is "my React or Vue site should serve HTML to crawlers through a hosted service", the package to install in your app is the middleware:

npm install prerender-node --save

There's one catch. The same README says: "If you're testing locally, you'll need to run the prerender server locally so that it has access to your server." If that's your case, or you want to run the server yourself, keep reading and fix the compiler.

If you'd rather not run the server at all, here's one option. We make RenderSwap, a hosted prerender service: your prerender-node middleware stays, and you swap the service URL and the token for the ones from your RenderSwap account. The Free plan covers 1 verified domain and 500 fresh renders or 1 browser hour a month, whichever comes first, with no card and no email to sign up. It renders only your own public pages, on domains you've verified, so it won't help with a localhost test.

Install the Visual C++ build tools

node-gyp's own README covers this. The quick route uses Chocolatey and installs Python and the Visual C++ workload in one go:

choco install python visualstudio2026-workload-vctools -y

For the manual route, the README says that for Visual Studio 2019 or later, you use the Desktop development with C++ workload. For anything older, it says to install Visual Studio Build Tools with the Visual C++ build tools option. Microsoft's page adds that if you want only the command-line toolset, you can download the Build Tools for Visual Studio.

  • Already have Visual Studio 2019 or later? Add the Desktop development with C++ workload to it.
  • Fresh machine, no Visual Studio? Use the Chocolatey line above, or Build Tools for Visual Studio if you want only the command-line toolset.
  • Installing Node.js anyway? The windows-build-tools project notes that "the official Node.js for Windows installer can now automatically install the required tools." Look for that while you run the installer.
  • On Windows on ARM? node-gyp says to add the components "Visual C++ compilers and libraries for ARM64" and "Visual C++ ATL for ARM64".

If you've seen advice to install windows-build-tools, check its repository page first. It now says: "This repository was archived by the owner on Sep 11, 2021. It is now read-only." Use the routes above instead.

Run npm install from a Developer Command Prompt

Installing the tools isn't always the end of it. Microsoft's page says: "The tools require several environment variables to be set. These variables add the tools to the path and set the locations of include files, library files, and SDKs."

  • Close every terminal, including your editor's built-in one.
  • Open the Developer Command Prompt for your version of Visual Studio. Microsoft's page says to type developer command prompt in the desktop search box, then choose the result you want.
  • Change to your project folder and run npm install again.
  • Don't copy the compiler folders into your system PATH by hand. Microsoft's page says: "We don't recommend you set these variables in the Windows environment yourself."

If the install now gets past the compile step, you're done. If it fails with a different error, read the first error line in the log, not the last one.

When node-gyp still can't find Visual Studio

If the tools are installed and node-gyp still doesn't pick them up, the README suggests installing a PowerShell module:

Install-Module VSSetup -Scope CurrentUser

In the README's words: "This will make Visual Studio detection logic use a more flexible and accessible method, avoiding PowerShell's ConstrainedLanguage mode."

You can also tell node-gyp which Visual Studio to use. Its --msvs_version option is described as "Set Visual Studio version (Windows only)". For one older toolset you need it: "Auto-detection fails for Visual C++ Build Tools 2015, so --msvs_version=2015" needs to be added. The README notes it's not needed when run by npm as configured in its install steps.

node-gyp configure --msvs_version=2015

Quick reference: which fix for which setup

Your situation What to do
You only need the middleware in your Express app Install prerender-node and point it at a hosted service
You want to run the prerender server yourself Install the Desktop development with C++ workload or Build Tools for Visual Studio
Tools installed, error still there Re-run npm install from a fresh Developer Command Prompt
node-gyp can't detect Visual Studio Install the VSSetup PowerShell module, or pass --msvs_version
Windows on ARM Add the ARM64 compiler and ATL components

  • {'text': 'Microsoft guide to the MSVC toolset on the command line', 'url': 'https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/building-on-the-command-line'}
  • {'text': 'prerender-node middleware setup guide', 'url': 'https://github.com/prerender/prerender-node'}
  • {'text': 'windows-build-tools archived repository page', 'url': 'https://github.com/felixrieseberg/windows-build-tools'}

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need the full Visual Studio IDE to fix "Failed to locate: CL.exe"?

No. Microsoft says that if you want only the command-line toolset, you can download the Build Tools for Visual Studio. node-gyp's README also gives a Chocolatey command that installs Python and the Visual C++ workload.

I installed the C++ tools and still get the error. Why?

Check your terminal first. Microsoft says the tools require several environment variables, and these variables add the tools to the path. Open a new Developer Command Prompt and run npm install again from there.

Is windows-build-tools still the way to install the compiler?

Its repository was archived by the owner on Sep 11, 2021 and is read-only. The same page says the official Node.js for Windows installer can now install the required tools, and node-gyp's README lists the Visual Studio routes.

Do I need the prerender package to use prerender-node with a hosted service?

Not going by the prerender-node README. prerender-node is the Express middleware, and it defaults to the service already deployed by prerender.io. You can set PRERENDER_SERVICE_URL or prerenderServiceUrl to use a different service. The README says that if you're testing locally, you'll need to run the prerender server locally so that it has access to your server.

articles.title: Why 4 Image Upscaling Creates 16 the Pixels
articles.author: daoming wen
articles.description:
Choosing “4×” in an image tool sounds straightforward. But that small control hides several different questions:

  • How large will the output be?
  • How much memory might processing require?
  • Does a larger image actually contain more reliable detail? Understanding the distinction helps developers build clearer interfaces and avoid surprising users. A scale factor applies to both dimensions For an image with width W, height H, and scale factor s: output width = W × s output height = H × s output pixels = W × H × s²

Consider a 1,200 × 800 image:
Scale Output dimensions Pixel count
Original 1,200 × 800 960,000
2× 2,400 × 1,600 3,840,000
4× 4,800 × 3,200 15,360,000

Doubling both dimensions creates four times as many pixels. Multiplying both dimensions by four creates sixteen times as many.

This relationship matters for upload limits, processing capacity, previews, and pricing.
Compressed file size is an incomplete resource limit
A small JPG can decode into a large image.

For the 4,800 × 3,200 output above, a single RGBA buffer with one byte per channel requires:
4,800 × 3,200 × 4 = 61,440,000 bytes
That is about 58.6 MiB for one buffer.

A processing pipeline may also hold the original image, temporary buffers, model tensors, and encoded output. The actual memory requirement depends on the implementation.

A file-size limit alone therefore cannot describe processing cost. Validate decoded dimensions and output pixel count as well.
Preview the result before starting
A useful confirmation interface can show:
Input: 1,200 × 800
Selected scale: 4×
Requested output: 4,800 × 3,200
Output pixels: 15.36 MP
If processing consumes credits or incurs a charge, show that amount alongside the dimensions.

These values should describe the exact request that will run. The server must validate them independently; the browser preview is a usability feature, not an authority for billing or resource limits.
Make oversized requests understandable
Suppose a request exceeds the processing limit.

Silently reducing the input and still displaying “4×” creates ambiguity. Users may reasonably interpret that label relative to their original file.

Clearer options include:

  • Rejecting the request with a specific explanation.
  • Offering a supported scale.
  • Showing the proposed reduced dimensions and asking the user to accept them. The important part is making the final dimensions visible before processing starts. Evaluate geometry and quality separately An image can have the correct dimensions while containing undesirable changes.

AI upscaling can infer plausible textures and edges. Those details are not necessarily faithful to the original subject, especially around small text, faces, and repeated patterns.

Use two separate checks:

  1. Geometry: Does the downloaded file have the promised dimensions?
  2. Visual quality: Are important details useful and believable at the intended display size? Keep the original file, compare at consistent viewing scales, and inspect more than one selected example.

For documents, evidence, and other accuracy-sensitive images, treat inferred detail with particular care.

A clear image interface makes the output dimensions, resource limits, and visual limitations understandable. The multiplier is only the starting point.

articles.title: Building a Lightweight Vietnamese Lo Ban Ruler Calculator with Vanilla JS
articles.author: Phong Thủy Thức Tâm
articles.description:
In Vietnamese architecture and interior design, the Lo Ban Ruler (Thước Lỗ Ban) is commonly used to check auspicious dimensions for doors, furniture, and home layouts. Instead of relying on heavy frameworks or external APIs, you can model all three standard Lo Ban rulers in just a few lines of Vanilla JavaScript using modulo arithmetic and lookup arrays.

Understanding the Three Ruler Cycles

Each Lo Ban ruler repeats periodically along a fixed length, divided into major segments (cung lớn) and minor sub-segments (cung nhỏ):

  1. 52.2 cm (Thông Thủy) — Used for clear openings such as doors, windows, and hallways (8 major segments of 6.525 cm, each split into 5 sub-segments).
  2. 42.9 cm (Dương Trạch) — Used for solid structures and furniture like desks, beds, and cabinets (8 major segments, 4 sub-segments each).
  3. 38.8 cm (Âm Phần) — Used for altars and memorial dimensions (10 major segments of 3.88 cm, 4 sub-segments each).

Core Modulo Calculation in JavaScript

To evaluate any input measurement mm against a ruler cycle cycleMm and an ordered array of segment definitions:

function checkLoBan(lengthMm, cycleMm, segments) {
  if (lengthMm <= 0) return null;
  // Normalize measurement into a single ruler cycle
  const posInCycle = ((lengthMm % cycleMm) + cycleMm) % cycleMm;
  const segmentSize = cycleMm / segments.length;
  const index = Math.min(
    Math.floor(posInCycle / segmentSize),
    segments.length - 1
  );
  return {
    positionMm: Number(posInCycle.toFixed(2)),
    segment: segments[index],
  };
}

By keeping the ruler definitions as pure JSON/array data and computing positions client-side in mm, the UI stays instantaneous even when dragging a virtual ruler slider in real time.

Live Demo & Source Code

We built an open-source, zero-dependency online lookup tool combining all three rulers (52.2cm, 42.9cm, 38.8cm) with instant search and visual scale rendering:

  • Live Demo: Tra cứu Thước Lỗ Ban Online
  • Source Code (GitHub): lequy240193/thuoc-lo-ban-phong-thuy
  • Project Homepage: Phong Thủy Thức Tâm

articles.title: 9 UX Fixes That Make OTP Verification Screens Convert Better (with Code)
articles.author: Authly
articles.description:
You can have the most reliable OTP delivery in the world and still lose users on the verification screen. Codes that are hard to type, resend buttons that don't work, and vague errors all cause drop-off at the exact moment someone is trying to sign up.

Here are nine fixes that make an OTP screen easier to complete, with front-end code you can copy. It pairs with my Node.js WhatsApp OTP tutorial, but the front-end works with any backend that has a "send code" and a "verify code" endpoint.

1. Use the right input types

Mobile keyboards matter. Use a telephone keyboard for the phone number and a numeric keypad for the code:

<input id="phone" type="tel" inputmode="tel" autocomplete="tel"
       placeholder="+1 415 555 2671" required />

<input id="code" type="text" inputmode="numeric"
       autocomplete="one-time-code" pattern="[0-9]*"
       maxlength="6" placeholder="123456" required />

autocomplete="one-time-code" lets iOS and some Android browsers suggest the code straight from the incoming message, so users don't have to switch apps and copy it.

2. Tell users where the code is coming from

"We sent you a code" isn't enough. If the code arrives on WhatsApp, say so:

We sent a 6-digit code to +1 415 555 2671 on WhatsApp.

Users who expect an SMS and never see one will assume the system is broken. Naming the channel prevents most "I didn't get my code" requests.

3. Show a clear resend timer

Let users request a new code, but not instantly, and show the countdown:

function startResendTimer(button, seconds = 60) {
  let remaining = seconds;
  button.disabled = true;
  button.textContent = `Resend code in ${remaining}s`;

  const timer = setInterval(() => {
    remaining -= 1;
    if (remaining <= 0) {
      clearInterval(timer);
      button.disabled = false;
      button.textContent = "Resend code";
    } else {
      button.textContent = `Resend code in ${remaining}s`;
    }
  }, 1000);
}

The countdown also reduces spam requests, which saves money on every message you send. Remember to enforce the cooldown on the server too, because anything in the browser can be bypassed.

4. Disable the button while the request is running

Double taps create two requests, two messages and two bills:

async function sendCode() {
  const sendBtn = document.getElementById("send");
  const phone = document.getElementById("phone").value.trim();

  sendBtn.disabled = true;
  sendBtn.textContent = "Sending...";

  try {
    const res = await fetch("/auth/send-otp", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ phone }),
    });
    const data = await res.json();

    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(data.error || "Could not send the code");

    window.otpId = data.otpId;
    showCodeStep(phone);
    startResendTimer(document.getElementById("resend"));
  } catch (err) {
    showError(err.message);
    sendBtn.disabled = false;
    sendBtn.textContent = "Send code";
  }
}

5. Verify automatically when the last digit is typed

Removing the extra tap on "Verify" makes the flow feel fast:

const codeInput = document.getElementById("code");

codeInput.addEventListener("input", () => {
  codeInput.value = codeInput.value.replace(/\D/g, ""); // digits only
  if (codeInput.value.length === 6) verifyCode();       // match your code length
});

async function verifyCode() {
  const code = codeInput.value;
  codeInput.disabled = true;

  try {
    const res = await fetch("/auth/verify-otp", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ otpId: window.otpId, code }),
    });
    const data = await res.json();

    if (!res.ok || !data.verified) throw new Error(data.error || "Invalid code");
    onVerified();
  } catch (err) {
    showError(err.message);
    codeInput.disabled = false;
    codeInput.value = "";
    codeInput.focus();
  }
}

Keep a visible "Verify" button as a fallback, for example for screen readers and people who paste a longer code.

6. Write error messages that help

Compare these:

Weak Better
"Error" "That code isn't right. Check it and try again."
"Request failed" "We couldn't send the code. Check the phone number and try again."
"Invalid" "That code has expired. Tap Resend to get a new one."

Keep messages helpful but not too specific about security details. For example, don't reveal whether an account exists.

7. Let users fix a wrong phone number

A typo in the phone number is one of the most common reasons codes never arrive. Always show the number the code was sent to, with a visible "Change number" link that returns to the first step without losing the rest of the form.

8. Offer another channel when the first one fails

If the user has waited and the code hasn't arrived, show a second option next to the resend button, such as "Send via Telegram" or "Send by email". Automatic fallback on the server helps, and a visible manual option covers cases where the user knows WhatsApp isn't available to them.

9. Don't forget accessibility and mobile

  • Put a <label> on every input
  • Use aria-live="polite" on the message area so screen readers announce errors
  • Make tap targets at least 44×44 px
  • Keep the page usable at 320px width
  • Don't rely on colour alone to show an error 
<p id="message" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p>

Quick checklist

  • [ ] Correct input types and autocomplete="one-time-code"
  • [ ] Channel and phone number shown on the code screen
  • [ ] Resend countdown, enforced on the server too
  • [ ] Buttons disabled while requests run
  • [ ] Auto-submit when the last digit is entered
  • [ ] Helpful error messages
  • [ ] "Change number" option
  • [ ] A second channel when delivery fails
  • [ ] Accessible labels and live error messages

Wrapping up

OTP screens are a small part of your product, but they sit in the path between a visitor and an account. Small UX improvements here usually lift completion rates more than tweaking the copy on your landing page.

For delivery over WhatsApp, Telegram and Email with automatic fallback, I'm building Authly, and the docs show how to wire up the backend. I'm the maker, and I'd like to hear which of these UX problems you've run into. Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: One calculator, 12 languages: the number-format bugs we hit (and the small helpers that fixed them)
articles.author: CasinoKit
articles.description:
We maintain a set of small free calculators (wagering, odds, expected value, withdrawal times and a few more) that run in 12 languages: English, Czech, German, Greek, Spanish, Finnish, French, Hungarian, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese and Romanian. Translating the labels was the easy part. The bugs that actually reached users were about numbers: separators, currency symbols, and amounts that silently stayed in the wrong currency.

This post collects the rules we ended up with and the short helpers behind them. The stack is React 18 + Vite with i18next, but nothing here depends on it.

Note: the calculators deal with probability and expected value. They are maths tools, not a recommendation to gamble (18+).

1. The URL decides the language, nothing else

Our first version mixed signals: browser language, a saved setting and the path. The result was German text on an English URL, which confuses people and search engines alike. The rule now is simple: the first path segment is the language, an unprefixed URL is English.

const NON_EN = ['no', 'de', 'fr', 'es', 'pt', 'fi', 'pl', 'ro', 'hu', 'cs', 'el'];

export function urlLang(pathname = location.pathname) {
  const first = (pathname.split('/')[1] || '').toLowerCase();
  return NON_EN.includes(first) ? first : 'en';
}

The browser language is still used, but only once: a human who lands on an English URL is sent to the same page in their language (navigator.languages, with nb/nn mapped to no). A language picked by hand in the menu always wins, and crawlers are never redirected, so every language keeps its own indexable URL.

2. Never build a number string by hand

"5,000" is five thousand in English and five in German. We had text like amount.toFixed(2) glued to a symbol in a few places, and every one of them was wrong somewhere. All numbers now go through Intl.NumberFormat with an explicit locale per language:

const LOCALE = {
  en: 'en-GB', no: 'nb-NO', de: 'de-DE', fr: 'fr-FR', es: 'es-ES', pt: 'pt-PT',
  fi: 'fi-FI', pl: 'pl-PL', ro: 'ro-RO', hu: 'hu-HU', cs: 'cs-CZ', el: 'el-GR',
};

export function formatNumber(n, lang, maxDigits = 2, minDigits = 0) {
  if (typeof n !== 'number' || Number.isNaN(n)) return n == null ? '' : String(n);
  let v = n;
  if (Math.abs(v) < 0.5 / 10 ** maxDigits) v = 0;            // no "-0,00"
  const text = Math.abs(v).toLocaleString(LOCALE[lang] || 'en-GB', {
    minimumFractionDigits: minDigits, maximumFractionDigits: maxDigits,
  });
  return (v < 0 && /[1-9]/.test(text) ? '-' : '') + text;
}

formatNumber(5000, 'de');  // "5.000"
formatNumber(5000, 'fr');  // "5 000" (narrow no-break space)
formatNumber(12.5, 'cs');  // "12,5"

Two details that cost us time:

  • Negative zero. -0.001 rounds to "-0" in some locales. The guard above turns tiny values into a clean 0.
  • Spaces are not spaces. French and Norwegian use a narrow no-break space (U+202F), others a normal no-break space (U+00A0). Any regex that parses a formatted number back must accept both, plus ., , and a plain space.

3. The symbol position belongs to the currency, not the language

"€40" and "40 €" are both correct, depending on where you are. "Ft 15 000" is not. We keep one small list of currencies whose symbol goes after the number, and the sign always goes in front of everything:

const POSTFIX = ['HUF', 'PLN', 'CZK', 'NOK'];

function money(amount, currency, symbol, lang) {
  const num = formatNumber(Math.abs(amount), lang);
  const body = POSTFIX.includes(currency) ? `${num} ${symbol}` : `${symbol}${num}`;
  return (amount < 0 ? '-' : '') + body;   // "-€40", "-19 200 Ft"
}

4. Store one base currency, convert at display time

All example values and limits are stored once, in EUR. Each language has a default display currency (Hungarian pages show forints, Polish pages zloty, Czech koruna, Norwegian krone), and the conversion happens only when the value is rendered:

const fromEur = (v, rate) => (typeof v === 'number' ? Math.round(v * rate * 100) / 100 : v);

Anything that is not a number passes through untouched. That matters more than it looks: a missing value must stay missing.

5. "Unknown" is not zero

This was our most embarrassing bug class. When a value was not published, an early version fell back to 0, and the UI proudly showed "€0". Now an unknown value is null all the way down and is rendered as a neutral "?" or a short translated notice, never as a number. We added a build check that fails when an unpublished limit or threshold is stored as 0 instead of null.

6. Free text with amounts needs the same treatment

Labels are easy because they live in translation files. Longer texts are harder: a sentence like "deposits from €20 up to €5,000" is written once per language and the amounts inside it must still follow the visitor's currency. We parse amounts with a regex that understands both symbol positions and all the separators from point 2, convert them, and format them again with the page locale. One rule saved us here: a leading zero means a decimal, never a thousands group ("0,003" is three thousandths, not three).

7. Test the formats, not just the maths

Our unit tests used to check calculate() and stop there. Most real bugs were in the last step, so our browser checks now open the calculators in a non-euro language (Hungarian or Polish) and read the visible string: correct separator, symbol on the right side, no NaN, no undefined, no stray English word. We also keep a build check that rejects English-style thousands ("2,000") inside non-English texts.

Summary

  • The URL is the single source of truth for the language.
  • Every number goes through Intl.NumberFormat with an explicit locale.
  • Symbol position is a property of the currency, the sign goes first.
  • Store one base currency and convert on render.
  • Unknown is null and is shown as "?", never as 0.
  • Test the rendered string in a non-euro language.

You can see all of this working in the calculators at casinokit.app/tools/: switch the language in the menu and watch the separators and currencies change.

articles.title: Celebrating ten years of Svelte
articles.author: Rich Harris
articles.description:
It started with a commit — specifically, this one. Ten years later, we’re far from done; software never is. But we’ve come an awful long way. Last week the community gathered in Ljubljana, at the third in-person Svelte Summit, to mark the anniversary.

To be completely honest, I expected the atmosphere to be a little subdued. Being enthusiastic about front end frameworks feels somewhat passé in the era of agentic coding and software factories, so a conference dedicated to one of the more boutique ones could easily have felt like a bit of a throwback.

But I was wrong. The energy was fantastic. We had two days of lively conversation and unbelievable demos in one of Europe’s most beautiful cities, with a slew of announcements that we’ll follow up on in more detail soon:

  • Custom renderers are now supported behind an experimental flag, allowing you to use Svelte to build native apps and terminal UIs and PDFs and just about anything else you can imagine.
  • Async Svelte is making real progress towards production readiness.
  • vite-devtools-svelte, which integrates with Vite DevTools, was moved into the Svelte organisation and is working towards a 1.0 release.
  • rsvelte, by Svelte core team member Yuichiro Yamashita, is a unified Svelte toolchain written in Rust. It’s not quite production-ready yet, but it is hilariously faster than the JavaScript equivalents.
  • Svelte is now a core framework for Storybook.
  • mdsvex, a markdown toolkit for Svelte components, reached version 1.0.

Naturally, we spent a lot of time talking about AI. Many of the announcements are directly relevant to agentic development (the devtools expose an MCP server, rsvelte makes it practical for fleets of agents to work on large apps concurrently, and so on), and most attendees described themselves as frequent — if ambivalent — users of the technology. But there’s nothing like an in-person gathering to remind you that the best bits of the job can’t be automated away.

Keep an eye on the Svelte Society YouTube channel, where the talks will be published in the coming days, starting with Unfinished business by yours truly.

We’re a decade in, and our best years are still ahead of us.

#​812 — November 24, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

Nudeps: Bundler-Like Imports, None of the Baggage — What if you could npm install a package and import it by name in the browser without a bundler? Lea and Dmitry Sharabin's new tool makes this easier than ever using import maps (which it keeps up to date). Run npx nudeps install and add the import map script to your HTML. There are also demos to try.

Lea Verou

💡 This work follows on from Lea's popular essay earlier this year: Web Dependencies are Broken. Can We Fix Them?

Agents Didn’t Clear Your Plate. They Dumped Reviews on It — Your agents write PRs in minutes, then eat your afternoon in review. When did ‘saving time’ start to mean babysitting agents’ work? Meticulous shows the exhaustive impact of every PR, with no developer effort. Devs at Dropbox & ElevenLabs have their afternoons back. You can too.

Meticulous sponsor

jQuery 4.1 Released (Plus a Goodbye to 3.x) — Most of us probably don't need it (just 16% of State of JS 2025 respondents use jQuery regularly) but it lives on in ~63% of sites, so if that includes yours, both releases fix a selector bug (that can hang the page) and 3.8 is 3.x's last planned feature release.

Timmy Willison (jQuery)

IN BRIEF:

  • Chrome 157/158's DevTools can now debug with original variable and function names (see above), including in minified code, if the source maps include data from the scopes proposal.

  • TC39 meets again next week (remotely this time). The agenda has text imports up for stage 4, immutable ArrayBuffers for stage 3, and AbortController-based cancellation for stage 2.

  • Ladybird, a 'truly independent' browser built from scratch (including its JS engine), is now in alpha. Simon Willison takes it for a spin here.

RELEASES:

  • webpack 5.113 – Building on its new built-in HTML and CSS support, webpack now scopes classes in <style module> blocks and updates matching names in the HTML.

  • 🔒 Bun 1.4.5 – A security release with fixes across HTTP/3, TLS, DNS and Zstandard, affecting Bun.serve, fetch, and several node: modules.

  • 🖼️ Jimp 2.0 – Image processing in pure JavaScript. A huge release that now also supports animated GIFs.

  • Nuxt 4.7, DOMPurify 3.5, Redux Toolkit 2.15, NestJS 12.6, vlt 1.8.1

📖  Articles and Videos

What Runs Your JavaScript? Engines vs Runtimes — Defining where a language ends and its supporting runtime begins can be tricky, especially for JavaScript with its unusual history and genesis in the browser. Mara explains the key moving parts, the difference between a host runtime and JavaScript itself, and how different JS implementations draw the line in various places.

Mara Averick

💡 The JavaScript engines zoo is worth a visit in its own right. It's a data table covering 139 JavaScript engines, their compliance, language they're built in, etc.

Foxit Compares 10 eSignature APIs — Embedded signing, webhooks, sandbox access, pricing and compliance, in one table you can shortlist from.

Foxit sponsor

Why I Switched to Vite+ — Is the unified Vite+ toolchain worth adopting? Ben, of the Vue core team, shares his impressions of how it works on his 97,000 line project and concludes it's worth the effort.

Ben Hong

Custom Renderers: Svelte Can Now Go Beyond the DOM — Svelte components can now render to WebGL, native UIs, or the terminal, say, with a 'custom renderer' telling Svelte how to create/update nodes there. It's experimental in Svelte 5.59 which just landed.

Paolo Ricciuti and the Svelte Team

💡 As an example of what this opens up, gpuix-svelte renders Svelte as a native desktop app using the Zed editor's GPUI. Yet another JS desktop/GUI app option!

Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS Limit for Canvas — Safari famously caps page updates to 60 FPS by default, even on iPhones that go higher. But Rida found a sneaky way to get canvas rendering and touch input up to 120…

Rida F'kih

📄 To Remove Moment.js, We First Made Everything Depend on It – Replacing ~1000 date-handling call sites without changing what users see across locales. Medhat Dawoud

📄 Chrome Prerendering is Weird – It can run your site's JavaScript before you've even hit Enter in the address bar. Tom Bennet

📄 What's New in Angular 22.3? Cédric Exbrayat

🛠 Code & Tools

Component Party: See What Changes in Solid 2 — The long-standing 'Rosetta Stone' of UI frameworks (well worth revisiting in its own right) now covers Solid 2, and you can see a 'before and after' of numerous code examples in 2 vs 1.

Mathieu Schimmerling

Solid 2.0: The Long Hold — Five years after 1.0, the signals-based UI framework is now stable with async built right into its reactivity graph (so return a promise from a computation and everything downstream just handles it). Ryan explains the thinking, and why the SolidStart metaframework has been retired.

Ryan Carniato

💡 Ryan expands on the latter point in The Metaframework is Dead. Long Live the Metaframework, a 20-minute ViteConf talk.

Build Durable AI Agents & Workflows in TypeScript — Open-source and fault-tolerant. Tasks pick up right where they left off, even through failures, restarts, or deploys.

Trigger.dev sponsor

vlt Opens Its npm Package Mirror to Everyone — Clean installs can spend a lot of time downloading package metadata, but vlt's registry serves much less of it giving installs that can take 20-70% less time. No account/token is needed anymore, so give it a spin and see if it suits your setup.

Erick Wendel (vlt)

Astrobook: A Minimal Storybook Alternative — An alternative to the popular UI component playground that supports React, Vue, Preact, Svelte, Solid, Lit, and Astro. The demo site includes multiple framework examples.

Ocavue

  • Replay Node 26 – A 'time-travel' build of Node.js (for Linux x86-64 only) that records a run so you can debug it after the fact.

  • 📈 Frappe Charts 2.3 – Simple, zero-dependency SVG charts. Adds axis titles.

  • 🎵 OpenSheetMusicDisplay 3.0 – A way to render MusicXML sheet music.

  • jest-dom 8.0 – Custom DOM matchers for Jest and Vitest (5+ only).

  • 🔒 Hijacked GitHub accounts are being used to exploit servers that aren't patched against a variety of React and Next.js flaws and publish stolen credentials publicly. Here's some of what to check.

Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents.

If your agents build for the web, they automatically slurp in best practices to not slopify the web. Do you use it? And if so, does it work well? Or do you even contribute? I'd really love to learn more about it because I expect people simply let Claude do its thing...

Guten Tag! Guten Tag! 👋

Have you heard that ariaNotify is now baseline newly available? And do you wonder if JPEG XL is better than AVIF? And what's your take on Safari's new adaptive dark mode?

Turn on the Web Weekly tune and find some answers below. Enjoy!

::: song by="Pablo" title="Modeselektor - Sónar Festival 2026" youtube="tXzWwMk-0Ak" I love Modeselektor, an iteration of Apparat as Moderat, and this trippy one long hour concert at Sónar is energizing. :::

Do you want to share your favorite song with the Web Weekly community? Hit reply; there are two more songs left in the queue.

Deno and Astro joined Cloudflare. Nuxt and Svelte belong to Vercel. Tailwind and Remix joined Shopify. Anthropic acquired Bun, and OpenAI got the people from Pierre Computer Company (I'm just calling them out because they do very cool stuff).

And then there's Geoff. Geoff as in Geoff Graham, the editor of CSS-Tricks. After DigitalOcean bought the site that we all visited daily from Chris Coyier, it looked like another project was going to die because DigitalOcean seemed to have lost interest in it.

Not with Geoff, though, because he bought back CSS-Tricks from DigitalOcean. I have no idea about the deal size, but, oh boy, I definitely didn't see this one coming. And, of course, Geoff has big plans!

I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of everyone, no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.

Many people shared that this feels like a long-awaited win for us, the bloggers, the educators. And I must admit I also felt a bit of encouragement after hearing the news. Maybe there's still a place for blogging, sharing, and learning together.

So, thank you, Geoff, for pushing forward. I really, really, really hope that this works out for you. And selfishly for us! ❤️

If you enjoy Web Weekly, share it with your friends and family.

  • 🦋 Bluesky
  • 🐘 Mastodon
  • 💼 LinkedIn

A quick "repost" really helps this indie newsletter out. Thank you! ❤️

Web Weekly Housekeeping

It's been quiet the last couple of weeks, so I want to apologize to my supporters for the silence. Thank you all for supporting Web Weekly on GitHub Sponsors and Patreon. ❤️

Something that made me smile this week

I don't know when or how I discovered Robert's blog. It feels very... wholesome? Browsing around gave me some good old blogging vibes. Robert also runs monthly themes, and this month's theme is "knowember".

If you're curious, here's my quick Knowember post.

Participate

No code

  • becoming yourself is a social project → "Most of us are surrounded by more care, intelligence, and help than we know how to access. Maybe part of reaching your potential is learning how to become easier to help."
  • Bug blindness → "I've seen people and teams with a high degree of quality blindness ship things that have reduced or even no chance of success because of product quality issues"
  • Writing to me with AI → "I really dislike this vibe on the internet right now. It feels like I’m constantly having to avoid being “tricked.”"

A nice abstraction

That's a nice quick tip. Lean described how to turn document.currentScript into an inline templating engine. Love it!

Replace it!

For the image nerds: JPEG XL vs AVIF

You might have heard that JPEG XL is now supported by all major browsers. Should you use it? Jake put out a massive article comparing the new format with AVIF. Be warned, the article is very long, but the tl;dr at the top has you covered.

Choose wisely

Should buttons have cursor: pointer?

So, do you use cursor: pointer for buttons? I'm strongly in favor of doing this, but as it turns out, some people have strong opinions on the matter.

Decide

Rebuilding flex-wrap: balance

flex-wrap: balance; is so far only shipping in Chromium. If you still want to achieve balanced flex layouts, Ahmad shared some ways to come up with similar results.

Be balanced

The wonderful weird web – The nicest place

If today's one of those days when you could use a hug, you'll find one at the nicest place on the internet. Love the old-school vibes of the site.

Get a hug

Upcoming: headingoffset

Granted, it's not prime time yet for headingoffset (shipping in Firefox 162 first) and :heading(), but adjusting heading levels is a feature we've needed since the failed outline algorithm. Let's see when the other browsers pick this up!

Control your headings

The Navigation API

The Navigation API has been available in all browsers since January. Do you use it?

If not, Ollie went on a tour to describe what you can do with it. The posts are quick reads and give you a good idea of what's possible. Thank you, Ollie!

  • The navigate event
  • Initiating navigations with the Navigation API
  • Focus Management with the Navigation API
  • Preventing same-document and cross-document navigation

.PropFLIP

If you've been in the game long enough, you might remember the FLIP technique. FLIP allows you to use CSS transitions for animations that you would usually need JavaScript for. Now, the technique is from 2015, so there must be a more modern version, right?

That's what Adam was after, and he describes a modern approach to FLIP using @property.

Flip it!

Move all these grid items

And speaking of moving things around, did you know that you can use and transition anchor-positioned grid items? That's some fancy stuff!

Move them

A fancy range slider

As usual, I've no idea how Temani does it, but what you see above is a CSS-only input of type range, an output element, and a label. I've got no words!

Pick a value

Safari's new adaptive dark mode

If you're a Safari user and are bothered by bright websites, Safari 27.3 beta introduced a new feature to automatically turn bright websites dark. The feature respects color-scheme so that it doesn't clash with your dark mode styles, and if you want to disable the feature entirely, <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> is your friend.

Go dark

And apparently, Chrome ships an auto dark mode feature behind chrome://flags/#enable-force-dark, too. I wonder how many bug reports come in when browsers change how sites look natively.

No AI Slop: A Manifesto

Nothing more to add here than some quotes from the manifesto.

Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it.

When an agent wrote something we're sending, we make that clear, and we check the parts that matter before it goes out.

Human time and attention is incredibly valuable, so we optimize for using it wisely.

Don't be a slop cannon

Random MDN – :state()

From the unlimited MDN knowledge archive...

I gotta be honest here: I hadn't seen :state() before. Dave explained how he uses "pseudo-pseudo-classes" to build interactive component demos and well... today I learned :state() is a web component thing.

Give state

New on the baseline

It feels like browser vendors are still on fire, and it's hard to keep up with all the new features shipping. So here are some calm and easy-to-digest baseline updates. 🫣

  • Baseline newly available: ariaNotify
  • Baseline widely available: AbortSignal.any

Classifieds & friends

Web Weekly reader David is working on Pour. Pour is a WCAG 2.2 accessibility audit engine written from the W3C specifications. If you care about accessibility, which I'm sure you do, you should check it out!

Three valuable projects to have a look at

  • syabro/neat-annotations – Hand-drawn CSS annotations for inline content.
  • vercel-labs/portless – Replace port numbers with stable, named local URLs.
  • nilbuild/tinyhand – A tiny hand on a stick that points at things on your Mac screen. 😅

A new Tiny Helper

Back in the day, some people had the hobby of doing CSS art with the goal to draw things in a single div. The trick was to use multiple box-shadow or background values on the elements. I never tried creating these, but it can't be easy.

If you want to get into the game for some relaxation though, "Gradient Layers" helps you create and debug all these CSS declarations.

Be a CSS artist

Find more single-purpose online tools on tiny-helpers.dev.

Thought of the week

I 100% agree with Robin's take here.

The developers who thrive in this era will not be the ones with the highest output. They will be the ones whose output other people are glad to receive. Everyone else is generating work and calling it productivity.

Minor Changes

  • BREAKING CHANGE: The animateExit() mixin now starts animations synchronously in beforeRemove instead of deferring them to a microtask. This allows animateLayout() to measure the updated layout when exiting elements are taken out of normal flow. (#12220)

    This is unlikely to be a breaking change for most consumers. Custom mixins used alongside animateExit() may be affected if they inspect computed styles or call getAnimations() in beforeRemove and rely on the exit animation starting later.

  • animateEntrance() and animateExit() mixins now support per-property timing and compositing overrides via the transition option. (#12220)

  • Validate native controls with a shared form schema using @remix-run/ui/form. form.Context supplies field bindings, and root, control, label, and error mixins provide native constraints, validation feedback, and accessible associations. Failed submissions restore values and display errors. Applications own the markup, and forms work with or without JavaScript. These experimental APIs may change or be removed in patch releases. (#11630)

  • Added @remix-run/ui/toast for accessible toast notifications. A shared manager retains notifications in the browser, with providers and mixins connecting them to your own markup after mounting. (#12084)

Patch Changes

articles.title: test v1.2.0
articles.author: github-actions[bot]
articles.description:
Minor Changes

  • t.useFakeTimers() now fakes Date, performance.now(), setImmediate()/clearImmediate(), and AbortSignal.timeout() along with the timer functions, so wall-clock code such as expiry checks and timestamps can be tested without injecting a clock. While fake timers are active, Date.now(), new Date(), and performance.now() read the fake clock and move forward only with advance() or advanceAsync(). new Date(value), Date.parse(), Date.UTC(), and instanceof Date keep working. Immediates fire on the next advance(), and AbortSignal.timeout(ms) signals abort with a TimeoutError once the fake clock reaches ms. (#12203)

    Like Node's mock timers, the fake Date starts at the Unix epoch (0) and performance.now() starts at 0. Tests that used fake timers while reading the real Date, or while relying on real immediates or AbortSignal.timeout(), now see fake time instead. Pass the new now option to start at a specific time:

    let timers = t.useFakeTimers({ now: new Date('2030-01-01T00:00:00Z') })

  • Added data-property mocking with mock.property() and t.mock.property(), including read/write records, one-access value overrides, and descriptor restoration. Added getter and setter spies through mock.getter(), mock.setter(), and the fourth mock.method() argument. Exported MockTracker as the shared type for standalone and test-context mocks. (#12225)

    Test-context accessor and property mocks restore in reverse installation order after cleanup callbacks, even when a test or cleanup callback fails. Method mocks layered over getter spies preserve the accessor's backing value. Method, accessor, and property mocks can be created while Array.isArray is mocked, with array argument checks preserved.

  • Added public TestFn and TestMeta types for reusable test callbacks and metadata, with linked API documentation for the test body and its options. (#12226)

  • Add new t.waitFor(condition, { interval, timeout }) API to retry assertions until they pass. Polling stops when the test ends. See Polling Assertions for usage. (#12224)

Patch Changes

  • Fix several gaps in t.useFakeTimers(): (#12203)

    • clearTimeout() and clearInterval() now cancel real timers created before fake timers were enabled. Previously the fakes ignored those timers, so a test with a timeout option that enabled fake timers left its real timeout timer running after it finished, which later aborted the test's signal and kept the process alive.
    • setTimeout() and setInterval() now pass extra arguments to the callback.
    • In Node, fake timers return handles with ref(), unref(), hasRef(), and refresh(), so code that calls .unref() on a timer no longer throws. Clearing an expired timeout's handle prevents refresh() from reactivating it.
    • Calling t.useFakeTimers() again restores the previous clock before starting a new one, so cleanup restores the original Date. Repeated restore() calls have no effect.
    • Restore fake timers synchronously on abort and before user cleanup callbacks. Finished or aborted contexts cannot enable another clock, and runner deadlines keep using real timers.
    • Reject overlapping clocks, roll back failed installations, and restore the original property descriptors without reinstalling fakes beneath spies. Restoration attempts every property, reports failures, and permits retrying failed properties.
    • Keep fake timer IDs unique across clocks so clearing a stale numeric handle cannot cancel a later test's timer.
    • Fake AbortSignal.timeout(ms) validates its argument synchronously using Node's numeric integer range of 0 through 4294967295 in every runtime.

  • Fix test and lifecycle hook timeouts stalling under fake timers and prevent late timeouts from aborting completed test signals. (#12224)

articles.description:
#​811 — November 17, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

npkill 1.0: Not Just for node_modules Anymore — npx npkill has long offered a way to find and remove waste from node_modules folders. Its first release in two years now also hunts down caches and build outputs like .next and .turbo, with 'profiles' for 20 ecosystems. If you're new to the tool, its homepage provides a good introduction.

Juan Torres

Agents Didn’t Clear Your Plate. They Dumped Reviews on It — Your agents write PRs in minutes, then eat your afternoon in review. When did ‘saving time’ start to mean babysitting agents’ work? Meticulous shows the exhaustive impact of every PR, with no developer effort. Devs at Dropbox & ElevenLabs have their afternoons back. You can too.

Meticulous sponsor

UI SDK: Headless UI Behaviors for React, Vue, Svelte, & Solid — A new library from shadcn and Vercel that provides 50+ accessible, low-level behaviors, like roving focus, typeahead, popups, and drag and drop, that you compose into components (for several frameworks, plus Web Components).

Vercel

💡 𝕏 As shadcn says: "You and I don't need the same interfaces. We need the same interface behaviors." The idea is an agent, say, can generate whatever UI suits a task, with reusable focus, keyboard, and accessibility behaviors built in.

IN BRIEF:

  • Solid 2.0 is now stable, with 2.0.0 now on npm and the docs updated to match. There's no official announcement post (beyond the earlier Solid 2.0 RC posts) so expect more on this soon.

  • The Chrome team has proposed a Cross-Origin Storage API for sites to share large assets like AI models and WASM modules, so users would only have to download them once.

  • The cloud-based JavaScript hosting service Val Town is winding down with services ending January 10 and the code being open sourced in February.

  • The Bun team has published a dense technical tour of how its in-development ahead-of-time compiler works.

RELEASES:

  • Prettier 3.10 – The code formatter now supports the latest JavaScript proposals and new Flow syntax, and adds an opt-in plugin that swaps in the Zig-based Yuku's JS/TS parsers for speed.

  • 🎨 p5.js 2.4 – The creative coding library expands its SVG and 3D model support. Here's a starter sketch if you want to play quickly.

  • 🔒 Node.js v26.13.1 (LTS), v24.22.3 and v22.23.5 – The security releases we mentioned last week fix an HTTP/2 flaw that lets clients crash a server and an HTTPS bug that can leak other connections' memory.

  • PixiJS 3D – The popular 2D rendering library's official 3D engine is now in open beta. It's WebGPU-first, with a WebGL 2 fallback.

📖  Articles and Videos

📊 e18e's Ongoing Benchmarks of JavaScript Meta-Frameworks — The e18e performance initiative tracks releases of frameworks across the ecosystem (e.g. Nuxt, Astro, SvelteKit, SolidStart, and more), measuring everything from install size and build times to rendering speed. This dashboard is the place to dive in.

e18e

🤖 The Top 10 Things AI Gets Wrong in Web Development — The Chrome team examines where coding agents fall back on dated techniques, like hand-rolled focus traps instead of inert and JS overlays instead of popover, alongside gaps in passkey implementations and XSS defenses. A handy checklist for humans too.

Philip Walton (Google)

AI Security for Modern JavaScript & TypeScript — Traditional tools miss logic gaps. SonarQube Hunter Agent catches broken access control in your JS/TS CI/CD pipeline.

SonarSource sponsor

How a Third-Party Script Turned Malicious on Major Sites — An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely's A/B testing platform to inject a (now removed) malicious script into pages served to end users. Scott's analysis found it on sites including Zoom, the BBC, and GitLab, and shows how CSP can, and did, help.

Scott Helme (Report URI)

💡 Third-party scripts are an increasingly common attack vector, as Polymarket's users recently found. If you load any, brush up on CSP and Subresource Integrity, and if you provide them, see how Fathom secures theirs.

How Promises Really Resolve, Explained via a WebKit Bug — A contrived promise that should have thrown instead caused Bun and Safari (both of which use JavaScriptCore) to hang. Alistair fixed the bug and uses it to explain what resolve() actually does and why resolved isn't 'a real promise state'.

Alistair Smith

The Web Is More Than Enough — A reminder of how the vast array of powerful web platform APIs enables the development of complex apps in the browser, particularly as AI reduces the headaches involved in tying them together.

Paul Ford

Your JS Error Is Lying to You — Why can JSON.stringify(err) unexpectedly leave you with {}? Gabor presents a tour of what an Error holds, and how much of that makes it through stack traces, cause chains, worker boundaries, and loggers like Pino and Winston.

Gabor Koos

📄 How 13,000 Local Variables in a Function Overflowed V8's Stack – And why would that ever happen? It was the output of an OCaml to JS transpiler… :-) Jérôme Vouillon

📄 A Universal XSS in uBlock Origin via Its Element Picker – Leans on an interesting (and now fixed) postMessage and iframe exploit chain. Smitty van Bodegom

📄 Migrating 10,144 Tests from Jest to Vitest in Three Weeks Daniele Rossino

🛠 Code & Tools

BrowserPod 4.0: A Linux-Like MicroVM for the Browser — A WASM-powered sandbox that runs Node, npm, git, and bash in the browser. Previously a metered service, v4.0 is free for any use, though it's not open source, and you must load it via their CDN (but no account or API key is needed).

Leaning Technologies

💡 Going somewhat deeper, Nitro creator Pooya Parsa has compiled the actual Linux kernel to WebAssembly (repo). It boots to a shell in under a second in modern browsers, or via npx unkernel (tip: use halt to exit!).

Debug Errors and Agents Faster: Sentry Changelog Live — A walkthrough of what’s new in debugging, from fixing prod bugs with Seer to tracing your agents. Register today.

Sentry sponsor

Kitesurf: Cloudflare's Browser Engine Now Open Source — An experimental browser for agents we featured in August. Mostly written in TypeScript and runs JavaScript in V8 isolates on Workers, with Rust compiled to WASM for layout and painting. There's no Chromium, and Puppeteer can drive it.

Cloudflare

File Viewer: A Multi-Format File Viewer for Internal Apps — Read-only views for Office, PDF/OFD, CAD, archives, email and other complex formats, with integrations for React, Vue, and Svelte. The docs site has demos showing off the formats covered.

Flyfish Dev

Flashwright: A Faster, API-Compatible Playwright Fork — Keeps Playwright's API and test runner, but reuses a browser context per worker and doesn't wait for animations to settle, plus similar tricks. Benchmarks show a ~2-4x speedup, while this post explains how it works.

Codebeast

React Flow 13: The Node-Based UI Library Gets Faster — The first major release in two years cuts re-renders in large flows, with new useNode and useEdge hooks. Vue Flow has joined the xyflow family too.

xyflow

  • SlickGrid 6.0 (above) – Long-standing data grid component. Now with zero dependencies, plus pinning on all four sides and sticky rows and columns. Examples and introductions on the project homepage.

  • XState v6 Beta – First beta of the state machine/actor library's next major version. The core API is considered stable and you can try it with xstate@beta.

  • 🕹️ Excalibur 1.0 – After 13 years, the 2D TypeScript game engine reaches v1 with 2D lighting, a plugin API, and a rebuilt Web Audio mixer. Sample games here.

  • 🕹️ JSNES 3.0 – JavaScript NES emulator. Now has a cycle-accurate core that passes all 134 'AccuracyCoin' tests. There are playable demos here.

  • type-fest 6.0 – Popular collection of essential TypeScript types (listed here). v6.0 adds 120 new types and requires TypeScript 6.

  • Fontkit 3.0 – Advanced font engine for Node and the browser. Now ESM-only, with a new core export so you can ship only the formats needed.

  • dts-bundle-generator 10.0 – A tool to tree-shake and bundle a project's TypeScript declarations into one file.

📰 Classifieds

📄 Parsing PDFs for a RAG or invoice pipeline? Foxit compares 10 document parsing APIs on output format, billing units and accuracy claims.

🌙 Agents can test mobile code at 3am. Expo Simulators gives them cloud simulators, so the loop runs while you sleep.

Stop being the middle manager for your coding agents. CodeAF runs the org, and only what no manager can settle reaches you. #1 on DeepSWE.

📢  Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • You Don't Need jQuery, the long-standing guide to replacing jQuery methods with plain JavaScript, has had a big v3.0 update. Internet Explorer fallbacks are out in favor of modern one-liners like el.replaceChildren(), structuredClone(), and Promise.withResolvers().

  • Adam Argyle shares PropFLIP, a take on FLIP (First, Last, Invert, Play) animations where four @property custom properties do the inverting and a CSS transition does the playing.

  • AWS has released AWS Emulator, an official local emulator you can point your AWS SDK or CLI at, covering hundreds of its service interfaces. It's largely aimed at agents, and was built with them too.

  • 🎂 Happy birthday to Svelte! Svelte turned ten years old on Monday (Rich Harris made its first commit on November 16, 2016).

articles.title: How X (Twitter) is rebuilding its web app
articles.author: Unknown
articles.description:
#​810 — November 10, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

How X (Twitter) is Rebuilding Its Web App — X is replacing 3 servers with one app built on React, Vite and Fastify. Yagiz, famed for his performance work on Node, explains the streaming architecture behind it, along with some bottlenecks they had to fix, like how hundreds of tiny JavaScript files slowed startup.

Yagiz Nizipli (X Engineering Blog)

Why Standard Webhooks Hit 118m npm Downloads a Month — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini all sign webhooks with Standard Webhooks, the open spec Svix started. That's one finding in the State of Webhooks 2027, where we scored 489 API companies on retries and signatures. Immediate download, no email required.

Svix sponsor

Parcel 3 Alpha: The Bundler Rewritten in Rust — A ground-up Rust rewrite of the popular bundler that the team reports is up to 100x faster than Parcel 2 at cold builds of React Spectrum. It runs as a standalone binary without Node, with support for native plugins written in Rust, Go or Swift, while JavaScript plugins run on an embedded QuickJS runtime.

The Parcel Team

IN BRIEF:

  • 📊 The State of JavaScript 2026 survey is now open. Share the features, libraries and tools you use and like, and discover a few new ones along the way. We'll share the results once they're out.

  • TypeScript 7's Go-powered compiler now has an experimental WebAssembly build which already powers an early TypeScript Playground v2.

  • ESLint now officially lints shell scripts with the @eslint/shell plugin adding ShellCheck-like rules for Bash, sh and mksh.

RELEASES:

  • Playwright 1.65 – The browser testing tool's test runner can now run under Bun, plus there's a new failures reporter.

  • Storybook 11 Beta – The UI component workshop gets more agent-ready, with official skills, Claude/Codex plugins, headless CLI tools, and more.

  • 🔒 Vite has disclosed a critical remote code execution flaw affecting dev servers exposed to the network via --host or server.host. Upgrade to 8.3.7, 8.2.5, 8.1.7, 7.3.8 or 6.4.6.

  • 🔒 Next.js 16.4.5 and 15.5.29 fix seven security issues, including a high-severity cross-tenant cache disclosure.

  • 🔒 Node.js security releases are due tomorrow (or shortly after) for the 26.x, 24.x and 22.x lines.

📖  Articles and Videos

Experiments with Multithreaded JavaScript — What would JavaScript look like if threads could share objects directly? Former TC39 delegate Erik Arvidsson explores three approaches: in a Porffor fork, as a TypeScript library with an ownership checker, and as an implementation of the TC39 structs proposal. Each has a playground to try.

Erik Arvidsson

The New JavaScript Features Between V8 14.6 and 15.6 — Node 27, released in alpha recently, is built on V8 15.6, and Joyee tours what that brings to developers, including Math.sumPrecise, new iterator methods, and some behavior changes in sorting, dates and promises, all with sample code.

Joyee Cheung

How to Build Your Own Automated Debugging Workflow — Connect your coding agent to Sentry and turn errors into fix PRs. See the guides and recipes in the resource hub.

Sentry sponsor

Spreading Liquid with three.js — A technical explanation of a 'liquid-spreading' effect originally built for a cosmetics site. The in-page demo is fun to play with and this could be handy if you want to create paint-like effects.

Misaki Nakano

Reviving Facebook's Abandoned JavaScript Optimizer — Prettier creator James Long put agents to work resurrecting Prepack, Facebook's attempt to make JavaScript faster by running it ahead of time. There's an experimental demo that shows off the gains on a sample React app.

James Long

Yavashark: Building a JavaScript Engine for 950 Days Straight — A solo developer's progress report on a Rust-based engine they're building that passes around 82% of test262 and can server-render a React app. There's a playground to try it for yourself.

Sharktheone

📄 A Fifth Object Shape Made the Same Loop Twice as Slow – V8's hidden classes and inline caches in action. Mohsen Fallahnejad

📺 ReactiveScript: Early Findings – A lengthy stream by Solid's creator on ReactiveScript, his experimental reactive UI language he first shared in 2021. Ryan Carniato

🛠 Code & Tools

EmbedPDF 3.0: A PDF Viewer for Any JavaScript App — An open-source PDF viewer for vanilla JavaScript, React, Vue, Svelte and Angular. The v3 rebuild offers a ready-made viewer, headless components for custom UIs, and a standalone PDF engine. Try the demo.

EmbedPDF

Embed an Office Editor Your App's AI Agent Can Use — DOCX/XLSX/PPTX editing in your app with your model and workflow. Agents make targeted edits, and users refine the file.

Thinkfree sponsor

chrome-capture: Record a Chrome Tab at 60-120fps to an MP4 File — It's been three years since we've linked to Paul Irish (once a frequent fixture in JavaScript Weekly!) but he's back with a neat, compact tool you can run with npx to record a Chrome tab at high quality including audio to an MP4 video.

Paul Irish

Text.js: React Apps That Render in the Browser Console — Really! A React 19 framework whose 'screen' is the DevTools console, with routing, keyboard input, layout primitives and ASCII fonts. Open the console on the homepage to try it, then bunx create-text-app if you're tempted. GitHub repo.

Anomaly

Jeasx 3.0: Server-Rendered JSX, Now Streaming — A minimal framework that uses JSX purely as a server-side templating language (with no React and no hydration) on top of Fastify and esbuild. v3 streams pages while async components are still loading and renders ~2x faster. Live examples.

Jeasx

  • Rolldown 1.3 – The Rust-powered bundler adds experimental support for import attributes, but there are breaking changes to be aware of.

  • jsdom 31.0 – The pure JS implementation of DOM/HTML standards adds a new CSS engine and switches to a Skia-backed canvas backend.

  • Remix 3.2 – The full-stack framework adds nonce-based Content Security Policy middleware.

  • Wiki.js 3.3 – Open source JavaScript and Node.js-powered wiki app.

📰 Classifieds

📺 JetBrains AI.js Day 2026: Frontend's scariest AI questions answered live on channel 13, Nov 13. Register now!

🔑 One subscription, a dozen people. Fingerprint shows how many devices are really behind each account. Try it free.

📢  Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • 📺 I've been enjoying Arjay McCandless's YouTube channel lately as he's been focusing on maxing out VPSes with different stacks (and often being surprised by the results). This time, he compares 22 combinations of JavaScript runtimes and frameworks to see how many users they can handle!

  • 🌙 Safari 27.3 beta introduces Adaptive Dark Mode, an opt-in feature that automatically darkens light websites that don't provide their own dark theme.

  • 🎨 Three.js creator mrdoob is posting daily visual experiments for Codevember, complete with live demos and source.

  • 💰 Cloudflare has handed out the first $301,300 of the $1M Vite Ecosystem Fund it pledged when VoidZero joined, spread across 44 projects and maintainers, including e18e.

articles.author: Unknown
articles.description:
#​809 — November 3, 2026

Read on the Web

JavaScript Weekly

The AI Cost of JavaScript Frameworks

Nolan Lawson had Claude build the same app five times in each of twelve JS stacks to test common "X is better for agents" claims. Costs varied significantly between runs, and Gautam Parab found that the observed cost ranges overlapped or touched for most pairs of frameworks.

But a clearer difference was in the median amount of JavaScript sent to browsers: 0KB for Astro, 18K for Hono+htmx, 36K for SvelteKit, and 115–142K for React Router, TanStack Start and Next.js. If you've gone "hands-free", Nolan asks, why stick to a particular stack you chose when you wrote all the code? His benchmark is on GitHub to try for yourself.

Nolan Lawson

Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill.

Master.dev sponsor

Why Is This Fingerprinting Script 'Creating Bioweapons'? — A crawl of sites to collect canvas fingerprinting examples (which you can see, visually, at fingerprint.garden) found an anti-analysis technique where JavaScript identifiers were named after… taboo topics, with a prompt hidden in invisible Unicode, all designed to make LLMs refuse to work on the code!

Veritas

💡 Canvas fingerprinting is a technique that uses quirks of how different clients render canvas elements, in order to distinguish browser environments.

IN BRIEF:

  • 😄 Bartosz shares a creative way to generate strings and run code without parentheses or quotes. Good old JavaScript fun!

  • 📊 GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report has TypeScript as the most used language on GitHub by contributors (with JS at third), and ~44% of merged TypeScript PRs showing AI involvement. Plus a lot more besides.

  • GitHub Actions will block pull_request_target by default in public repos from December 2, unless an event policy explicitly allows it, with brownouts on November 9 & 16.

  • Cloudflare Workers now supports the Temporal API natively behind a temporal compatibility flag. It'll be available by default from December 1.

RELEASES:

  • Node.js v27.0 (Alpha) and v26.13.0 (LTS) – Node 26 is now the 'Lithium' LTS line, and 27 is the first ever Node 'alpha'. Under Node's new release process, every line spends six months in alpha before going Current.

  • Vitest 5.1 – A new --since-last-run flag reruns only tests affected by your edits, plus there's an interactive snapshot review feature.

  • Rspack 2.3 – The Rust-based webpack alternative adopts SWC Next and its rewritten parser. The team reports 5-20% faster builds and less peak memory use.

  • Leaflet 2.0 Beta 1 – The mapping library's first major in a decade goes tree-shakeable, ships TypeScript types, and drops its default export.

  • Effect 4.1, pnpm 12.17, ESLint 10.14.0, Nuxt DevTools v4

📖  Articles and Videos

"No, npm, 'estee' is not a typo of 'testem'" — Shane tried to publish a CLI called estee and hit npm's typosquatting filter, which (as best as we can tell) rejects names within a small Levenshtein distance of popular packages' names.

Shane Friedman

Shrinking clarity.js: When Cleaner Code Gzips Worse — Microsoft let an agent run 50+ size experiments on its analytics script. A big win came from dropping import * namespace objects, while good-practice refactors like extracting helpers actually made the gzipped output bigger.

Manu Nair (Microsoft)

Workshop: How to Implement Session Replay — Filters, custom tags, and sampling settings for finding the sessions that matter. Nov 5, 10am PT.

Sentry sponsor

'Nothing Installs at Our Company Until It's a Week Old' — Many recent package hijacks were caught within hours, so Bruno's company now makes new releases wait a week. He explains what this approach broke, what cooldowns don't stop, and settings for popular package managers.

Bruno Jurković

Timing Ten Design Systems, Then Fixing the Slow Ones — Den timed ten design systems (MUI, Ant Design, and Ionic among them) opening a 249-option select and ticking 100 checkboxes, then profiled the slow ones to find out why.

Den Odell

Using Bun? Dependabot Can't See Most of Your Dependencies — GitHub's dependency graph doesn't parse bun.lock, so Dependabot alerts cover only direct dependencies. Nicolas has some tips for improving matters.

Nicolas Charpentier (Shortcut)

articles.title: Blake Watson on the state of the industry (#note)
articles.author: Unknown
articles.description:
Here's Blake sharing his feelings about AI, software development and where we're all heading. He wrote the article that's been on my TODO list for a while. Let me comment on some highlights.

I feel like I will be able to build things I never have been able to before, but at the same time, I have heightened fears about being replaceable or less valuable in my job. If all I’m doing is prompting an AI bot, why am I being paid so much?

100% this. I'm scared and worried that the skills I put so much time into building are worth nothing. I used to be proud of my deep platform knowledge. Turns out Claude knows more.

And on a bigger scale, "personal software" is really happening. My friends are building browser extensions and websites for their fantasy football leagues. They don't care about quality as long as it gets the job done. Occasionally they ask me things about the DOOM (DOM), which is funny and scary at the same time.

At what point does software still need someone who actually knows what they're doing? I guess we'll find out soon enough.

If you haven’t used one of these coding tools in the last six months, you probably don’t have a good idea of what they are capable of.

I admire people who are still holding out against this technology, I really do. If that's you, you rock! Unfortunately, I couldn't agree more with the statement above.

If your arguments about LLM quality and all the generated fake news (hallucinations) are based on Copilot tryouts around last Christmas, you'd better check again. Things have changed a lot.

I just have this icky feeling when I use it.

Same. I hate that I can create things without effort or understanding. I hate that there are days when I talk to agents all day. I hate that it seems like nothing matters anymore. I hate that everyone is pushing and pushing and pushing and nothing gets done.

I’m worried about being replaced, but maybe I’ll be even more valuable. [...] So I just go back and forth. I worry about it, but then I think everything will work out.

Yes. There are good weeks and then there are bad weeks.

Sometimes, I'm okay with "focusing on the outcome". Sometimes, I'm fine with the loss of the job that was my favorite thing to do. Sometimes, I have enough energy to change habits and find satisfaction and joy elsewhere.

But sometimes, man... sometimes the new world drives me nuts.

So, let's hope Blake is right and things will work out (somehow).

Reply to Stefan
